1	---
2	name: extract-from-conversations
3	description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
9	taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
10	dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
11	what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
15	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
16	
17	## The goal
18	
19	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
20	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
21	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
22	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
23	
24	## Where the conversation comes from
25	
26	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
27	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
28	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
29	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
30	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
31	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
32	
33	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
34	when a session is done enough to mine.
35	
36	## What to look for — the friction signals
37	
38	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
39	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
40	
41	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
42	
43	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
44	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
45	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
46	
47	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
48	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
49	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
50	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
51	correctly **without the round-trip**.
52	
53	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
54	
55	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
56	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
57	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
58	convention and had it corrected in review.
59	
60	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
61	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
62	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
63	first, not after a detour.
64	
65	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
66	
67	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
68	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
69	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
70	
71	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
72	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
73	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
74	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
75	was already optimal.
76	
77	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
78	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
79	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
80	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
81	loss of quality.
82	
83	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
84	
85	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
86	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
87	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
88	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
89	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
90	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
91	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
92	
93	## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch
94	
95	Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:
96	
97	- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
98	- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
99	  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
100	  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
101	  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.
102	
103	The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
104	stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
105	every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
106	breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.
107	
108	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
109	
110	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
111	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
112	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
113	
114	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
115	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
116	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
117	
118	**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
119	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
120	**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
121	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
122	silence it replaced.
123

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
59	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. This is the first rung to try for any
60	   lesson whose whole logic is "these patterns over these files", and most captured conditions are. Give it
61	   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
62	   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
63	   else's next change, not this run's.
64	2. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
65	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
66	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
67	   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
68	   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
69	3. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
70	4. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
71	
72	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
73	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
74	both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
75	[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
76	
77	**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
78	exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
79	derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).
80	
81	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
82	relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small.** Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every
83	session in every repo that declares the pack, forever, whether or not it ever applies — so a pass adds *at
84	most two*, each one sentence: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence clause only where the rule can't
85	be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph to land has not been understood well enough to be
86	a rule yet; the evidence behind it belongs in the PR body and the issue, never in the rule.
87	If more than two candidates clear every bar above, write the two strongest and drop the rest — they will
88	recur if they were real.
89	
90	When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
91	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
92	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
93	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
94	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
95	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
96	
97	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
98	trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
99	run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
100	rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
101	tidy-repo pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
102	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
103	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
104	
105	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
106	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
107	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
108	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
109	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
110	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
111	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
112	
113	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
114	
115	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
116	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
117	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
118	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

1	---
2	name: extract-from-conversations
3	description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
9	taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
10	dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
11	what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.
12	
13	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
14	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
15	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
16	
17	## The goal
18	
19	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
20	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
21	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
22	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
23	
24	## Where the conversation comes from
25	
26	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
27	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
28	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
29	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
30	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
31	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
32	
33	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
34	when a session is done enough to mine.
35	
36	## What to look for — the friction signals
37	
38	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
39	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
40	
41	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
42	
43	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
44	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
45	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
46	
47	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
48	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
49	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
50	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
51	correctly **without the round-trip**.
52	
53	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
54	
55	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
56	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
57	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
58	convention and had it corrected in review.
59	
60	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
61	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
62	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
63	first, not after a detour.
64	
65	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
66	
67	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
68	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
69	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
70	
71	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
72	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
73	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
74	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
75	was already optimal.
76	
77	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
78	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
79	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
80	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
81	loss of quality.
82	
83	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
84	
85	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
86	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
87	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
88	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
89	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
90	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
91	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
92	
93	## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch
94	
95	Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:
96	
97	- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
98	- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
99	  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
100	  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
101	  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.
102	
103	The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
104	stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
105	every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
106	breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.
107	
108	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
109	
110	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
111	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
112	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
113	
114	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
115	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
116	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
117	
118	**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
119	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
120	**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
121	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
122	silence it replaced.
123

1	# Extracting lessons — the bar and the local promotion ladder
2	
3	> **Scope: what both extraction skills share.** This doc is the **bar** a lesson must clear and the
4	> **ladder** it descends once it clears it — the half that is identical whatever the lesson was mined
5	> from. What each *source* adds is owned by its own skill:
6	> [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) for commits, merged PRs and issue
7	> activity, and [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) for a session's
8	> dialogue. Both load this doc; neither restates it.
9	
10	Its callers are the growth pack's [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md) daily task, which runs
11	both skills over one window, and an owner's occasional plain-words ask for a retrospective.
12	
13	## Run the pass on a capable model
14	
15	Extraction is mechanical, but deciding *what clears the bar* is a judgment call a weaker model fails
16	silently — it ships a plausible-but-wrong "lesson" where a capable model correctly bails (see
17	[the unattended-agents skill](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md), "Match the agent model to the judgment it
18	must make"). The terse rules that *govern* the pass — run it, plus the separate efficiency analysis — also
19	live there; this doc is the how-to.
20	
21	## From signal to lesson — the bar
22	
23	A signal is only worth writing down when the fix is **durable, reusable, and generalizable beyond this one
24	session or window.** Before adding anything:
25	
26	- **Dedupe ruthlessly** against the existing packs — a lesson already covered (even worded differently,
27	  even in another pack, even enforced by a check) is not a new lesson.
28	- **A dedupe miss has a second reading**, and when the candidate rule names an identifier you don't
29	  own — a function, field or setting — it is the likelier one: grep that identifier in the
30	  dependency's **code** before landing anything. No hit usually means the mechanism was retired and
31	  the rule is *expired*, not that the lesson is novel.
32	- **One-offs don't qualify.** A situational detail, a restatement of a generic truism, or something already
33	  implied by an existing rule is below the bar.
34	- **Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission, security, or classifier denial.** A
35	  pattern of "it was denied, then succeeded on retry" is real signal about *reliability*, not license to
36	  write a rule instructing every future session to retry, ignore, or explain past such a denial without
37	  asking — however solid the retry evidence looks, that shape of lesson never clears the bar. Report a
38	  recurring denial to the owner instead; a checked-in instruction that tells unattended sessions to bypass
39	  a safety gate is a standing bypass with no consent behind it, however it got there.
40	- **Promote what's portable.** A lesson true for projects beyond this one belongs in shared, cross-project
41	  canon, not stuck in one repo's local packs — the growth lifecycle's promote stage lifts it there
42	  centrally; capture it well locally and let promote generalize whatever travels.
43	
44	## Route to the local pack that owns it — the promotion ladder
45	
46	A project's capture surface is its **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/<pack>/`); everything else
47	under `.claudinite/` is the read-only mounted canon and is never a capture target. Pick the pack whose
48	territory the lesson belongs to (most repos have one general pack; some segregate a domain pack), then
49	prefer the strongest mechanism it allows:
50	
51	**First check whether a canon pack already owns it, from the catalog and not from the mount.** A repo
52	holds only the packs it *declares*, so "nothing here covers this" is a fact about the mount rather than
53	about the corpus — and acting on it homes the lesson locally in territory a canon pack already owns.
54	Read `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md` (canon-side `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`),
55	which states every canon pack's boundary including the ones this repo doesn't hold. Where the owning
56	pack's stated territory is merely too narrow, propose widening it rather than routing around it.
57	
58	1. **A declared check** — an entry in that pack's `declared-checks.json`, whose `failureMessage` *is* the
59	   lesson. Nothing wires it: writing the declaration adds the check. This is the first rung to try for any
60	   lesson whose whole logic is "these patterns over these files", and most captured conditions are. Give it
61	   `severity: 'blocking'` and `since: '<today>'`: the engine holds a check to advisory for its first two
62	   weeks, so a check may land against a tree that still violates it and the backlog it surfaces is somebody
63	   else's next change, not this run's.
64	2. **A custom code rule** — a `<rule>.mjs` exporting `run(ctx)`, listed on the pack's `pack.mjs` — only
65	   when the check needs what patterns can't say: real parsing, structured-data field logic, git/diff or
66	   conversation state, a derived comparison. Reaching for code where a declaration would do costs a module
67	   to read and maintain for nothing. An **unattended** run ships one `advisory`: hand-written logic has
68	   failure modes a declaration cannot have, and nobody reviewed this one.
69	3. **A pack skill**, when the lesson is an activity-scoped procedure rather than a condition.
70	4. **Terse prose** in the pack's `RULES.md` — the fallback, only what none of the above can carry.
71	
72	Either check rung ships with a **red-first fixture**; the declaration vocabulary is documented in
73	[`pattern-rules.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs)'s header, and the authoring shape for
74	both rungs — with the `since` grace window — in
75	[`engine/checks/README.md`](../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule).
76	
77	**Two check shapes are below the bar however cleanly they'd be written**: one that asserts particular code
78	exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time and reds the next legitimate edit), and one
79	derivable from the product's own requirements (that is a requirement — it belongs in the tests).
80	
81	Write **more checks and less prose**: a check relieves every session's context completely, where prose only
82	relocates it. **Prose is rationed, and the ration is small.** Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every
83	session in every repo that declares the pack, forever, whether or not it ever applies — so a pass adds *at
84	most two*, each one sentence: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence clause only where the rule can't
85	be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph to land has not been understood well enough to be
86	a rule yet; the evidence behind it belongs in the PR body and the issue, never in the rule.
87	If more than two candidates clear every bar above, write the two strongest and drop the rest — they will
88	recur if they were real.
89	
90	When no pack's scope fits, the lesson lands in the repo's general local pack. A **new** local
91	pack is justified only by the repo's own **project structure** — a segment of the repo's tree whose work is
92	its own territory (a `client` pack for work under `client/`), so a repo's local packs mirror its layout.
93	**Never mint a local pack around a technology or a methodology**, however real the knowledge: capture those
94	lessons in the structural pack that owns the work, and let the canon-side promote stage — Claudinite's call,
95	never a member's — decide whether a technology or methodology facet earns a pack of its own.
96	
97	**A gotcha tied to one call site is not a pack rule at all, and it is not this pass's to land either.** A
98	trap from misusing a specific API, class, or library belongs as a comment at that usage site — and a capture
99	run's write surface stops at its own packs, so **drop the candidate** rather than inflate it into a pack
100	rule or collect it into a centralized gotchas list. The comments in a repo's own source belong to the
101	tidy-repo pack's `improve-comments` task, which has its own trigger and its own review surface. Reserve a
102	central gotchas doc for what no single usage site owns: a trap you could hit *without* reading the relevant
103	file (a mistake of omission), or a cross-cutting invariant.
104	
105	**Two kinds never become a pack rule, however strong the evidence** — filter on what the lesson is *about*
106	before picking a mechanism. (1) **The owner's own preferences** — which word authorizes a merge, tone, how a
107	summary is shaped. They belong to the person, are injected per session from their own preference file, and
108	change without any repo hearing about it; a pack copy goes stale silently and then contradicts the live one.
109	(2) **The agent framework's own loading mechanics** — which packs are declared, why a skill didn't mount, why
110	an injection missed. That's engine plumbing, not project knowledge: a real defect there is filed upstream, and
111	writing it down as a project rule preserves the bug instead of fixing it.
112	
113	## "No new lessons" is a valid — and common — result
114	
115	Most sessions and most windows yield nothing durable, and that's the expected outcome. Say so and write
116	nothing rather than padding the docs to look productive: a spurious or duplicative "lesson" pollutes the
117	canon and costs every future reader. **Default to no edit when unsure** — the bar is a genuinely new,
118	reusable insight, not a diary of what happened.

1	# canon-curation
2	
3	Claudinite's own curation duties — the fleet-facing work only **Claudinite** runs: promoting
4	members' lessons into the shared canon, sweeping the fleet's stacks for technologies the canon does
5	not yet home, and policing the corpus's `packs/` tree. (The
6	prose-to-checks backlog sweep is no longer canon-only — it moved to
7	[claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md) as a per-repo task with a
8	`pack_paths` config, so every repo sweeps its own packs and Claudinite also its core `packs/`.) A
9	**local pack** of the canon home
10	(`.claudinite/local/packs/`, by owner decision 2026-07-19: Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite is
11	project-specific content, so it lives on the home's own capture surface, not in the portable
12	canon): `detect: null`, never seeded by `--init` or any migration, declared by hand in exactly one
13	repo — the canon home itself, as `local/canon-curation`. Its `tasks/<name>/` folders are found by
14	the home repo's own scheduler exactly like a canon pack's.
15	
16	**Declaration cardinality is the mechanism.** A pack's tasks run once per *declaring* repo, so a
17	pack only the home repo declares yields exactly one work item per task per occurrence — "central,
18	once" with no bespoke orchestrator step. Un-declaring the pack freezes canon absorption without touching
19	the members' side ([claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md)).
20	
21	| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| `growth-promote` | a participating member changed its local packs in the window | a PR against Claudinite's `main` |
24	| `growth-discover-packs` | weekly, over every covered member | a PR against Claudinite's `main`, plus an adopt issue in each member that evidenced the pack |
25	
26	| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
27	|---|---|
28	| Pack prose: no enforcement narration | check `pack-no-enforcement-narration` |
29	| Pack edit bumps pack version | check `pack-version-bumped` |
30	| Packs import only own + engine | declared barrier `pack-independence` ([declared-checks.json](declared-checks.json) — a `forbidReferences` entry; the [barriers pack](../../../../packs/barriers/README.md) documents the edge vocabulary) |
31	
32	- **[tasks/growth-promote/](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)** — the growth lifecycle's central stage: read the changed members'
33	  local packs, **generalize** the portable lessons, route each to the right canon home, and open a
34	  PR for the owner to approve. When a portable lesson's technology has no pack home, it mints a
35	  fingerprinted **stub pack** (in its own dedicated PR). This is the sole judgment gate before
36	  shared canon.
37	- **[tasks/growth-discover-packs/](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)** — the weekly **fleet sweep** for
38	  technologies the canon does not yet home: read every member's stack, fold the members into one view
39	  (so first-sight dedup is free — the third member using a technology is the same gap as the first),
40	  and open an owner-reviewed PR authoring the missing `packs/<tech>/`. A pack is authored because
41	  particular members' files demonstrated it, so each of those members also gets an issue asking it to
42	  adopt the pack once the PR merges and its mount carries it. It is the only stage that authors a pack
43	  at all — a member's local packs are what adoption seeded, and growth-extract writes rules into those.
44	  (Promote's stub-minting is narrower still: one lesson's technology, minted as a seed; this task
45	  authors from the whole fleet's usage.)
46	- **[item-routing.md](item-routing.md)** — the shared worthiness + routing method promote (and an
47	  owner-requested retrospective pass) defers to, so every decision about admitting and placing an
48	  item is made the same way.
49	- **[promote-scope.mjs](promote-scope.mjs)** — the CI write-surface gate on promote's PRs: promote
50	  may write only under `packs/` and `skills/` (keyed on the `growth-promote` branch prefix).
51	
52	## The growth lifecycle — three independent stages, no barriers
53	
54	How a lesson is learned in a consuming project, lifted into the shared canon when it's portable,
55	and pruned back out of the project once the canon owns it. Two packs split it by who declares them:
56	**[claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md)** (member-side: extract + dedup + pack
57	discovery, seeded, opt-out by removal) and **canon-curation** (this pack, the central stage).
58	
59	```
60	EXTRACT   per member    → auto-merging PR against the member's main   (claudinite-growth)
61	PROMOTE   central, once → PR against Claudinite's main                (canon-curation)
62	DEDUP     per member    → PR against the member's main                (claudinite-growth)
63	```
64	
65	All three are ordinary, **independent** planner units — there is no barrier and no phase ordering.
66	Each stage reads only what is already **merged**: promote processes whatever sits on members' mains
67	when it runs, so a lesson extracted tonight is promoted **tomorrow** night (the extract PR's merge
68	shows up in the next night's local-pack signal), and reaches other members' dedup once the promote PR
69	is approved and merged. That approval was always the dominant latency, so the barrier machinery bought little;
70	if the cadence ever matters, promote can run more often (twice daily, or before and after the
71	nightly) without any design change.
72	
73	**Review gates by blast radius, not uniformly.** Promote opens a PR — it's the sole judgment gate
74	before the shared canon every repo reads, so it always needs a human eye. Dedup opens a PR too — a
75	wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson. Extract lands through an **auto-merging PR** against the
76	member's `main` — it writes only that project's own local packs, so it earns a CI gate and a PR trail
77	but not a human reviewer; auto-merge keeps the fleet's daily lesson-capture from flooding review
78	requests. (An owner-requested, in-session retrospective delivers a PR for a human to review — see
79	[extracting-lessons.md](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/extracting-lessons.md).)
80	
81	**Central execution, no plumbing.** Promote runs from the Claudinite home repo with a fleet-wide
82	token, so it reads every participating member and opens its canon PR directly here — no
83	consumer-side Action, no cross-repo PAT, no labelled-issue up-path. The planner hands its gate the
84	`fleetMembers` aggregate (which members changed, and what they declare), and the gate hands the
85	worker the changed participants as `targets`.
86	
87	**This pack's tasks reach every member, so they name the wider invocation endpoint.** Both tasks
88	here declare `invocation_endpoint: 'fleet'` — a key into this repo's own
89	`taskScheduler.endpoints`, mapping to a routine whose sources are this repo **and every
90	participating member**. That cross-repo reach is the whole reason a second endpoint exists, and is
91	exactly what must stay off the endpoint an ordinary hand-off calls.
92	
93	Reach is a property of **which endpoint is called**, and of nothing else: there is no session scope
94	anywhere in the system, and no label routes a hand-off ([the writing-tasks skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)).
95	The `session_scope: 'fleet'` these tasks used to declare lost its last reader with the slot
96	scheduler and is gone from both.
97	
98	The failure mode moved with the mechanism, and moved in the right direction. A misconfigured
99	endpoint used to be **silent and permanent**: a dispatch label nothing picked up, re-armed hourly,
100	repeating forever with no comment anywhere. Now the hand-off is a synchronous API call, so an
101	endpoint this repo has not configured — or one whose token secret is unset — converges the item to
102	`needs-human` naming what is missing, on the item itself. If promote or discover-packs has quietly
103	stopped producing anything, read its most recent work item; the reason is written there.
104	
105	The session-scoped sibling of this nightly lifecycle — mining a single working session for lessons
106	— lives with [the growth pack's extract-from-conversations skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
107	(applied by the conversation half of its growth-extract daily task over captured logs), and the
108	member-side method docs (extract, dedup, and how a project's local packs are
109	identified) live with [claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md).

  authors from the whole fleet's usage.)
- **[item-routing.md](item-routing.md)** — the shared worthiness + routing method promote (and an
  owner-requested retrospective pass) defers to, so every decision about admitting and placing an
  item is made the same way.
- **[promote-scope.mjs](promote-scope.mjs)** — the CI write-surface gate on promote's PRs: promote
  may write only under `packs/` and `skills/` (keyed on the `growth-promote` branch prefix).

## The growth lifecycle — three independent stages, no barriers

How a lesson is learned in a consuming project, lifted into the shared canon when it's portable,
and pruned back out of the project once the canon owns it. Two packs split it by who declares them:
**[claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md)** (member-side: extract + dedup + pack
discovery, seeded, opt-out by removal) and **canon-curation** (this pack, the central stage).

```
EXTRACT   per member    → auto-merging PR against the member's main   (claudinite-growth)
PROMOTE   central, once → PR against Claudinite's main                (canon-curation)
DEDUP     per member    → PR against the member's main                (claudinite-growth)
```

All three are ordinary, **independent** planner units — there is no barrier and no phase ordering.
Each stage reads only what is already **merged**: promote processes whatever sits on members' mains
when it runs, so a lesson extracted tonight is promoted **tomorrow** night (the extract PR's merge
shows up in the next night's local-pack signal), and reaches other members' dedup once the promote PR
is approved and merged. That approval was always the dominant latency, so the barrier machinery bought little;
if the cadence ever matters, promote can run more often (twice daily, or before and after the
nightly) without any design change.

**Review gates by blast radius, not uniformly.** Promote opens a PR — it's the sole judgment gate
before the shared canon every repo reads, so it always needs a human eye. Dedup opens a PR too — a
wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson. Extract lands through an **auto-merging PR** against the
member's `main` — it writes only that project's own local packs, so it earns a CI gate and a PR trail
but not a human reviewer; auto-merge keeps the fleet's daily lesson-capture from flooding review
requests. (An owner-requested, in-session retrospective delivers a PR for a human to review — see
[extracting-lessons.md](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/extracting-lessons.md).)

**Central execution, no plumbing.** Promote runs from the Claudinite home repo with a fleet-wide
token, so it reads every participating member and opens its canon PR directly here — no
consumer-side Action, no cross-repo PAT, no labelled-issue up-path. The planner hands its gate the
`fleetMembers` aggregate (which members changed, and what they declare), and the gate hands the
worker the changed participants as `targets`.

**This pack's tasks reach every member, so they name the wider invocation endpoint.** Both tasks
here declare `invocation_endpoint: 'fleet'` — a key into this repo's own
`taskScheduler.endpoints`, mapping to a routine whose sources are this repo **and every
participating member**. That cross-repo reach is the whole reason a second endpoint exists, and is
exactly what must stay off the endpoint an ordinary hand-off calls.

Reach is a property of **which endpoint is called**, and of nothing else: there is no session scope
anywhere in the system, and no label routes a hand-off ([the writing-tasks skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)).
The `session_scope: 'fleet'` these tasks used to declare lost its last reader with the slot
scheduler and is gone from both.

The failure mode moved with the mechanism, and moved in the right direction. A misconfigured
endpoint used to be **silent and permanent**: a dispatch label nothing picked up, re-armed hourly,
repeating forever with no comment anywhere. Now the hand-off is a synchronous API call, so an
endpoint this repo has not configured — or one whose token secret is unset — converges the item to
`needs-human` naming what is missing, on the item itself. If promote or discover-packs has quietly
stopped producing anything, read its most recent work item; the reason is written there.

The session-scoped sibling of this nightly lifecycle — mining a single working session for lessons
— lives with [the growth pack's extract-from-conversations skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
(applied by the conversation half of its growth-extract daily task over captured logs), and the
member-side method docs (extract, dedup, and how a project's local packs are
identified) live with [claudinite-growth](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/README.md).

{"number":1353,"title":"Delete the updates/ shims, once no member's vendored worker names them","body":"The second half of L4. #1352 deleted the `engine/scheduler/` shims and repointed the update worker at `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/*`; the `updates/*` re-export tree itself is still there, deliberately.

## Why it could not go with the first half

The worker resolves its flows against a **fresh canon clone at HEAD**, not the member's own mount:

```js
git(['clone', '--depth', '1', CANON_URL, tmp]);
const load = async (rel) => import(pathToFileURL(join(tmp, rel)).href);
```

So the surface a member calls is whatever **its vendored worker** names, resolved against whatever canon looks like at that moment. Every member vendored a worker naming `updates/*` on 2026-08-24. Deleting the tree before they field the repointed worker fails their next update at module resolution — and nothing can repair it, because the repair *is* the update. That is the failure `basics/RULES.md` names: *"Changing an export in `updates/*` — empty it, never remove it."*

## The gate

**No member's vendored worker names `updates/`.** Read it off the members, never off this repo's tree and never off a date:

```
.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/worker.mjs
```

on each member's default branch — every one must call `load('packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/…')`. A member still on the old spelling has not converged past #1352 yet, and deleting the tree strands it.

That gate is met only after every member converges to `claudinite-lifecycle 60824.6` or higher, so the check is worth making after the fleet has had a night.

## What to do when it is met

- Delete `updates/` whole — `engine-update.mjs`, `pack-update.mjs`, `terminals.mjs`, `install.mjs`, `legacy-entry.mjs`, `README.md`.
- Drop the three `updates/*` entries from `install.test.mjs`'s `fielded` map, leaving the `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/*` ones. The comment there explains why both were listed; it comes out with them.
- Check whether anything else names the old path first — at the time of writing, the worker was the only live caller.

{"number":1169,"title":"Dissolve docs/skill-usage-metrics/DESIGN.md into the packs that own its subjects","body":"The owner's read, and it holds up against the tree: this design doc collapses into the pack that collects the signals and into the dashboard. It is 769 lines describing a pipeline that is now built, and the canon's own rule for that is already written — *behaviour belongs in the module header and the pack README*, not in a doc that has to be kept in step with both.

The evidence, section by section (line counts from `2026-08-21`):

| § | Lines | Where it already lives, or should |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Where knowledge lives | 16 | A standing architectural rule ("the canon knows mechanisms, never repos") — belongs with the local pack's standing decisions, not in one initiative's doc |
| 2 Sources of truth | 18 | `claudinite-growth/README.md` |
| 3 Capture (3.1–3.5) | ~100 | `claudinite-growth/README.md` already carries the capture lifecycle and retention almost verbatim; `capture-log.mjs`'s header carries the rest. **§3.4 (capturing an unattended session, where no SessionEnd hook fires) and §3.5 (the ordering constraint) are the one part with no other home** — they go into the pack README beside the lifecycle they belong to |
| 4.1 Check activations | 101 | Duplicated: `usage-fold/README.md`'s "The check failures are the win" and `fold-usage.mjs`'s header both carry the three marks, the CI-in-the-loop rule and the floor property |
| 4.2 Task invocations | 69 | Describes the retired slot-scheduler census. Keep two sentences of it as history in `usage-fold/README.md` (which already has them) and drop the rest |
| 4.3 Exec statuses | 16 | `usage-fold/README.md` |
| 5 The per-repo aggregate + shape | 146 | Duplicated: `usage-fold/README.md` and `usage-format.mjs`'s header |
| 6 The fleet aggregate | 63 | Superseded; **deleted outright** — the task it describes goes in #1166 |
| 7 Consumers | 40 | Split: the promotion-ladder half to `claudinite-growth/README.md`, the reader half to `claudinite-dashboard/README.md` |
| 8 TTLs | 12 | `claudinite-growth/README.md` (it already states retention) |
| 9 Failure modes | 45 | Duplicated: `usage-fold/README.md`'s "Failure is visible, never silent" |
| 10 + the two later rounds | 57 | Owner decisions with their rationale. These are the doc's only irreplaceable content — move them to the local pack's standing decisions, where a session actually reads them |

So the shape of the change: **almost nothing is written fresh.** Two sections move (§3.4/§3.5, and the decision record), one is deleted, and the rest is verified as already-covered and then dropped. If a section turns out *not* to be covered where this table claims, write it into the pack — do not keep the doc alive for it.

## The references are the real work

Eight files point into this doc by section number, and a dangling `§` pointer is worse than no pointer:

{"number":1496,"title":"Verify in production: the executor's `toJSON(vars)` line does not get the workflow held for approval","body":"Original-issue: #1492
In-production-when: `missingbulb/Claudinite` has at least one `Claudinite executor` workflow run whose head sha is `e846728` or later (the squash of #1494, which put `CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}` into `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`).
Verify: List those executor runs. PASS = every one of them created at least one job and none concluded `action_required`. FAIL = any run concluded `action_required`, or concluded in about a second having created zero jobs — that is GitHub's malicious-workflow hold, and it means `toJSON(vars)` is flagged the way `toJSON(secrets)` was in #1336.
Not-before: 2026-09-01T06:15:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day
Model: sonnet

## Why this could not be watched now

#1494 added one static line to the executor's work step:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}
```

The reader is fully unit-tested against synthetic JSON, so nothing about *parsing* a bag needs production. What no test can reach is the claim the whole change rests on: **that serialising the `vars` context does not trip GitHub's [malicious-workflow detection](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-07-28-github-actions-holds-potentially-malicious-workflows-for-approval/)** the way serialising `secrets` did in #1336.

That claim is inference plus field evidence, not a guarantee:

- GitHub publishes no detection signals, thresholds or false-positive rate.
- `vars` is the context GitHub's own docs define as non-sensitive and render unmasked in build logs, so the exfiltration reading does not apply — but that is our reasoning, not GitHub's statement.
- `packs/static-website/stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml` and `static-site-deploy-pages.yml` have both passed `toJSON(vars)` since before the safeguard shipped without a park — strong evidence, from a different workflow than this one.

The failure mode is why this is worth a run rather than a shrug: a held run creates **zero jobs** and concludes `action_required` in about a second, which from the queue's side is indistinguishable from "nothing was pickable". #1336 ate executor runs in two repos for hours before anyone noticed, and #1330 mis-diagnosed it as a repository setting. Nothing red appears. Only reading run conclusions finds it.

The canon's scheduler is on `44 5,17 * * *`, so its drain dispatches the executor twice a day; `Not-before:` is aimed just past the first tick after the merge.

## Instructions to the run

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the Actions API — the real run list, never a merge, a green CI job or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`.
   - Passes: comment the run ids and conclusions you actually read, and close this issue as completed.
   - Fails: reopen #1492 with a comment naming the held run, its conclusion and its job count, and say that `toJSON(vars)` must come out of `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml` and `packs/claudinite-tasks/stubs/claudinite-executor.yml` — the fleet is exposed to a silent park until it does. Comment here linking that, then close this issue as completed.
3. **Not yet live** (no executor run at or past that sha) → set `Not-before:` to the instant you are reading this at plus `Retry-every:`, clear this issue's `task:status:*` label, and leave it open. No comment.

```

```

## What this proves

The whole point of the change: the scheduler was **71% of private Actions spend** at ~26 min/day per member, because Actions bills each job rounded up and the cron fired 24 times a day to do about 13 minutes of work. Two ticks a day should make that ~2 min/day. Nothing so far has measured a real repo — only the simulator.

## What makes this step's world ready

#1235 closed (every member on the new cron), **and** at least one full UTC day has elapsed since, so there is a complete day to count.

## What to observe

For each **private** member — the ones that cost anything; public repos are free and unlimited:

1. **The count.** Scheduler workflow runs for one complete UTC day. Expect exactly **2**. Baseline: 24.
2. **Nothing was dropped.** No task's standing item is missing its occurrence for that day — a cheaper cron that quietly stopped instantiating work is a regression, not a saving.
3. **The risk the simulator could not model.** A whole day's chain now settles serially inside one executor run. Read the longest executor run's duration against the workflow's `timeout-minutes: 350`. The simulator's task durations are fixtures, so this is the first real read of whether a member's day actually fits.

## What counts as this step having worked

Every private member shows 2 scheduler runs for the measured day, no missing occurrences, and no executor run near its timeout.

## When the check fails

Comment what you read and **leave this issue open** — closing releases the next link.

- Still 24 runs on some member → its workflow never landed; reopen #1235's question there rather than proceeding.
- Missing occurrences → this is a real regression in the cadence change. Reopen #1225 with what is missing and stop the chain.
- An executor run near the timeout → do **not** fail the step, but say so plainly on #1225: it is the residual risk the plan named, and it wants its own issue rather than silence.

## How it ends

Comment the per-member figures on #1225 — runs/day before and after, and the longest executor run — then close this issue as completed. That close releases Link 3.

{"number":1509,"title":"Re-open the withhold lane: a member's workflows are no longer static after adoption","body":"#1494 put `CLAUDINITE_VARS: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}` into the executor stub. Every member holds the reader as of `claudinite-tasks` 60831.3, and **not one holds the line** — because nothing delivers `.github/workflows/` any more.

## The premise that closed the lane is now false

The withhold-and-hand-to-the-agent path shipped in #649 and worked. `packs/claudinite-canary-repo/migrations/2026-08-14-workflow-probe-current/` is documented as *"the first record to materialize into `.github/workflows/`"*.

#1317 closed it on one stated ground, at `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/pack-update.mjs:238`:

> Nothing needs to: a member's workflows are static after adoption (#1317).

That was true when it was written. #1494 is the counterexample: a workflow change every member needs, with no route to them. The alternative on the table was 13 hand-opened PRs — which the canon's own standing decision rejects, because per-repo manual work reliably does not happen.

## What is actually still there

The lane was **emptied, not removed** — the `updates/*` convention, and exactly the reason it exists. All four seams survive:

| Seam | State |
|---|---|
| `registry.mjs` `WITHHOLD_CAPABLE_ENV` / `WORKFLOW_DEST` / skip-with-note | intact, live |
| `pack-update.mjs` `PENDING_DIR`, `stagedAt()` | emptied, addressable |
| `stagedFiles()` | live — the sweep uses it |
| `applyStageFor(specs, withheld)` | still takes and renders `withheld` |

What #1317 removed is four lines: `write` drops workflow paths (`:239`), `env: {}` makes the handshake permanently false (`:242`), the sweep deletes anything staged (`:266`), and `withheld` is hardcoded `[]` (`:311`).

**The credential question is settled.** The Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` can never push under `.github/workflows/` — that part of the doctrine is real, and GitHub rejects the whole ref, so writing one into a tree about to be pushed fails the entire converge. But the apply stage does not run on that token: it raises a work item for an agent session, and the Claude GitHub App carries `workflows: write`. That is what closes the loop, and it is why staging + apply-stage is the shape rather than a direct write.

## A false green found on the way

`applyMaterializations` guards workflow dests and reports `SKIPPED …(workflow file; this caller cannot deliver one)`. `applyRewrites` (`registry.mjs:140-155`) has no such guard:

```js
if (next !== text) { await write(file, next); done.push(file); }
```

`write` silently drops workflow paths, but `done.push(file)` runs regardless — so **a rewrite record targeting a workflow file reports success while writing nothing.** Nothing has hit it because no record rewrites a workflow yet; this change makes that the exact shape needed, so it must be fixed here. Two structurally-identical surfaces, one guarded.

## The work

1. `applyRewrites` gets the same guard and the same skip-with-note as `applyMaterializations`.
2. `pack-update.mjs` refills the four seams: stage workflow paths under `PENDING_DIR`, announce the handshake, collect the real `withheld`, and scope the sweep so it clears pre-existing staged files without deleting what this run just staged.
3. A `claudinite-tasks` migration record rewriting the executor to insert the `CLAUDINITE_VARS` line — a **rewrite**, not a materialize, so each member's own stamped `# claudinite:secrets` names survive. It carries `applyStage` so a session delivers the staged file.
4. Forced fleet delivery afterwards, since this is an engine-flow change.

-# Growth — discover local packs (per repo)
-
-A weekly reflection on **this repo's own** captured knowledge: knowing the Claudinite packs already available to it, notice when project-specific knowledge is worth organizing into a **new local pack** — and author it. A local operation: it writes only the repo's **own** `.claudinite/local/packs/`, landing through a PR **a human reviews** (unlike [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md), which lands unreviewed where the repo's delivery settings allow; the shared canon stays human-gated too — lifting a local pack up is the central promote task's job). Finding nothing new worth a pack is a perfectly good, common outcome.
-
-There is no windowed Context to bind — the opportunity is standing (knowledge that was never organized into a pack, not a recent change), so examine the repo as it is.
-
-This run opens a PR and **never arms auto-merge**. Extract may land unreviewed because it adds prose or a rule to territory a local pack already owns; a **new pack** ships new `.mjs` conformance checks that run at every Stop and in CI the moment it merges — a check can break CI, so it's reviewed, exactly as the sibling [prose-to-checks-sweep](../prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md) is.
-
-## Conventions used in this doc
-
-- **GitHub access is MCP-only** (`mcp__github__*`) for issue/PR work; read the repo's own tree from the working checkout (local git), never a cross-repo clone.
-- **The repo's local packs** are everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename window) — the repo's own packs.
-- **The available canon packs** are the read-only mounted shelf under `.claudinite/shared/packs/` — what Claudinite already homes for this repo. Knowing the shelf is how you avoid re-creating locally what the canon already covers.
-
-## The pipeline
-
-### 1. Manifest the repo's own stack
-
-Catalogue what this project is built on and how it ships — grounded in its files (dependency/build manifests, lockfiles, toolchain/config, CI and release workflows, packaging/signing scripts, source structure, docs), citing the concrete evidence. Do **not** yet consult the pack shelf or decide anything about packs — this step only observes.
-
-**Never infer from "projects like this usually…"; if the repo doesn't show it, it is not in the manifest.** If something is present but appears vestigial or aspirational (declared but unused), include it and say so. Be **comprehensive over concise**: a later step filters and decides, so a true item you omit is lost, while an over-included one is cheaply dropped. When unsure whether something rises to an entry, include it with the `?` flag.
-
-Catalogue across **three axes**. Put each item under the single axis that fits best; when it genuinely spans two, place it under the primary and cross-note the other.
-
-- **Technologies** — languages and their versions, runtimes, frameworks, build systems, and the major libraries that shape how you write and build here (the load-bearing ones, not every transitive dependency).
-- **External services / APIs** the project integrates with.
-- **Deployment / distribution mechanisms** — how it ships and to where.
-
-For **each** item report: **name**; **axis**; **evidence** (the file(s), and what they show); **what it is in this repo** (one line); **prominence** — one of `core` (the project is built on it), `supporting` (used but peripheral), `vestigial` (present but apparently unused); and a **`?` flag** if you are uncertain the item is real or correctly characterised. Prominence is a factual read of how central the item is *in this repo* — **not** a judgment about whether it deserves any downstream treatment. Output the manifest as Markdown grouped under the three axis headings, one bullet per item with the fields labelled.
-
-### 2. Find the gap — what is pack-worthy but unhomed
-
-Now hold the manifest against two things: the **available canon packs** (`.claudinite/shared/packs/`) and the repo's **existing local packs**. The manifest feeds two separate decisions:
-
-- **What to declare.** A technology any canon pack already homes — **a stub pack included** — is **homed**: the action is *declare that canon pack*, never re-create it locally; note it.
-- **Whether a new local pack is warranted.** A new **local** pack segments by the repo's **project structure only**: a segment of the repo's own tree (a top-level `client/` or `server/`, a self-contained sub-project) whose work the repo genuinely does (not `vestigial`) and carries real, reusable working knowledge for — a build/config gotcha, a recurring project-specific procedure — that **no canon pack homes** and **no existing local pack captures** (if a local pack owns that territory, a new rule belongs in it — that's [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md)'s job, not a new pack).
-
-**Never mint a local pack around a technology, a domain, or a methodology** — however real the knowledge. A tech- or methodology-shaped lesson the canon doesn't home lands as rules/checks/skills in the local pack whose *segment* owns the work (the repo's general pack when it has no segments); deciding that such a facet earns a pack of its own is Claudinite's call, made canon-side by the promote stage over what the local packs captured.
-
-### 3. Author the local pack — distilled from the repo's real usage
-
-For each candidate, author a populated pack under `.claudinite/local/packs/<name>/`, distilled from **how this project actually works** — never from imagination. Apply the [generate-project-instructions](../../skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) method (don't re-derive it): descend the promotion ladder ([engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md)) — a rule a deterministic check can carry becomes the **check plus a see-it-fail fixture** (fires on a violating input, quiet on a clean one), a procedure with a nameable trigger becomes a skill, and only signature-less judgment lands as `RULES.md` prose. Ground and cite every rule in the project's real files. **Never pad** with speculative best-practice rules the evidence doesn't demonstrate; a rule you can't ground, you don't write — a smaller honest pack beats a padded one. And **never open an empty stub to fill later**. Write the pack files (`RULES.md`, `pack.mjs`, `README.md`), register it, and **declare it** in the repo's `.claudinite-settings.json` so it actually activates.
-
-### 4. Open the PR for review
-
-Land the new pack (and its declaration) through a single PR on a per-run-unique branch (see [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)) — title `Claudinite growth: discover local pack <name>`, and **put the issue reference in the commit message**: `Refs #<n>` for this task's tracking issue (below), in the commit itself, not only the PR body, so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. **Never arm auto-merge** — the reviewer is the point. A new check must still ship green (see it fail on a violating fixture, pass on a clean one) so CI stays green and the reviewer has something mergeable; a rule that can't be made a confident check lands as prose instead.
-
-## Record
-
-Everything this run has to say goes in the PR body, where the reviewer deciding on the pack is already
-reading: the repo segment the pack covers and the rungs its rules landed on, a candidate you found nothing
-groundable for, a "should declare canon pack X instead" note. A local pack carries no changelog file, and
-there is no standing issue.
-
-A run that authored no pack writes nothing anywhere.
-
-## What this task must never do
-
-- **Never touch the shared canon or another repo** — it writes only this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.
-- **Never re-create locally what a canon pack already homes** — declare the canon pack instead, and note it.
-- **Never mint a technology, domain, or methodology pack** — new local packs segment by project structure only; whether such a facet earns a pack is Claudinite's canon-side call (the promote stage).
-- **Never author from imagination or pad, and never open an empty stub** — every rule traces to the project's real usage; a pack may be small, it may not be invented.
-- **Never add a rule to a territory an existing local pack already owns** — that is growth-extract's job; this task is for *new* packs.
-- **Never conflate steps 1 and 2** — the manifest step catalogues and never consults the pack shelf; the gap step is where the shelf and the pack decision come in.
-- **Never arm auto-merge** — a new pack's checks reach every session and every CI run in this repo; the reviewer is what stands between a wrong check and a red repo.
-- **Treat the reviewer as a backstop, not a substitute** — judging pack-worthiness and authoring a pack (checks and fixtures included) is heavy judgment; get it right rather than leaning on the review.
